newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian economy looks abroad for breath of life.
newsitem.headline: Albanian economy looks abroad for breath of life.

text.p: With a Socialist victory in Albania's general elections all but certain, experts said on Wednesday the impoverished nation now had to address its most basic problem: rebuilding its shattered economy.
The reformed ex-communists face a staggering task as they prepare to clinch power from President Sali Berisha's right-leaning Democratic Party, which has ruled Albania for five years.

Months of unrest sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid funds earlier this year have undone what little progress Albania had made on the road towards a free market system after it emerged from 45 years of Stalinism in 1990.

Today, Albania's economy lies in ruins, its institutional infrastructure dismantled. Disillusioned foreign lenders and investors, who just a few years ago regarded the small Balkan state as one of the most promising candidates for early recovery, have turned their backs on Europe's poorhouse.

"The first issue for the Socialists is to proceed with a free market economy and build strong macroeconomic structures," said a senior U.S. administration official who oversaw Sunday's first round of the country's fourth multi-party election.

Western governments as well as international financial institutions have promised they will help deliver Albania from the economic abyss, but they insist the government must first provide a safe foundation on which to build.
"Unless we have some sound political framework in this country, we won't commit any money," said a Western diplomat.
The International Monetary Fund has disbursed some $60 million in credits to Albania since 1992, but the programme was suspended in 1995. The World Bank has dished out some $300 million in loans.
Compared to Albania's gross domestic product of barely $2.3 billion last year, the sums are substantial.
But placed next to the hefty $1.2 billion in savings wiped out by the crash of the pyramid fund, they seem paltry.
Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano has promised Albanians he will do all he can to reimburse investors for their losses. Quite how he will do so is another matter.

A planned law to control investment funds has fallen prey to pre-election political bickering. But even if adopted, many Western observers doubt it will have much effect in a country where a safe and sound banking system remains a distant vision.

"We will find some special sources to help Albanians recover from their losses," Nano said shortly after claiming his party's victory even before official results had been announced, adding international help was a key requirement.
Details of his economic agenda are sketchy. The Socialists insist they have thrown their communist heritage overboard and are now firm believers in capitalism with a kinder face.

But in a country where industrial production is almost zero and much of the population depends on small-scale agriculture to eke out a miserable living, there is little substance on which a Western-style economy could be built.

While a handful of the country's mid-sized industries were sold off in 1995, the planned voucher privatisation of Albania's large-scale industry has run into a brick wall, with the vouchers currently trading at 1.7 percent of face value.

Output, which just three years ago grew a healthy 10 percent, is expected to shrink by the same amount this year. Inflation is raging and forecast to top 70 percent by the end of the year. The lek currency has shed some 80 percent of its value against the dollar since January.
Albania is back to the starting point of its painful transition to a free market economy, but without international help, it is unlikely to reach the goalpost any time soon.

"We're very open to the programmes of the World Bank or the IMF, even the unpopular ones, to help restart our economy," said Nano. "But we're a small country with huge resources and it doesn't need much effort to restore normality."
